Toronto decides whether you get a bed by reading a thermometer. Below −5 °C it
opens extra space. Above it, it takes that space away.

There is no temperature at which a person outside is fine. Hypothermia does not
need freezing air. People with Raynaud's lose circulation in their hands well
above 20 °C, and cold injury makes it worse for the rest of their lives. A line
at −5 °C is not where harm starts. It is where the City decided to start paying
attention.

Everyone needs a place to be, every night of the year. What follows is drawn from
the City's own Auditor General and from six winters of its published records.

## The beds were made and the door was shut

When the thermometer rises, a warming centre "deactivates." Staff stop letting
anyone new in at 9 a.m. They spend the rest of the day moving the people already
inside back into the regular system. The building is open. The beds are made. No
one else is allowed in.

> "Since Warming Centres do not admit new clients while deactivating, beds were
> left vacant as the remaining clients were discharged."

That practice left **4,331 bed-nights** unused. Counting the other ways capacity
was withheld that winter, the auditor's own table reaches **12,742** bed-nights
that a change in practice could have freed. That is one winter, in a city where
people were outside every night of it.

## That same winter, 174 people a night were told there was nothing

The auditor, on the 2023/24 season:

> "There were 174 people, on average, who called Central Intake daily but were
> unable to be matched to a bed."

We checked that against the City's published Central Intake records for the same
winter and got 173.98 a night, across the 153 nights from 15 November to 15
April. Over the 94 nights the City was emptying those beds, that is about
**16,400** times someone asked for a bed and was told no.

## The ones turned away at the door are not counted at all

If you walk up to a warming centre and are told there is no room, that is
recorded nowhere.

> "TSSS does not track the number of people who walk into a Warming Centre or
> Winter Respite Site but are turned away when beds are not available.
> Consequently, the total demand for beds for TSSS' winter programs is not
> known."

The auditor asked staff whether it happens. They said it happens daily.

> "Staff at several of these programs advised that they turned some people away,
> with staff at three Winter Respite programs and one Warming Centre indicating
> that their program turned people away on a daily basis during the winter."

Every figure the City publishes about how many people need shelter is therefore
smaller than the reality, and the City states this itself: total demand "is not
known." A couple who phone together are recorded as a single call rather than two
people, which reduces it further.

## Most of the city is barely searched

The City counts people outside on a single day. It only searches places where
somebody is already known to be sleeping. Anywhere nobody is known about is left
out.

Downtown, 81% of the areas were searched. In Etobicoke–York, 38%. Each area a
team covered out there was nearly five times the ground of one downtown. In
Etobicoke–York they found one person outside an encampment across 181 square
kilometres.

The City searches hardest where it already has services, then uses what it finds
there to decide where services should go.

Scarborough and Etobicoke–York are **58% of Toronto's land**. On a cold night
they have **4.95 free low-barrier beds between them**. Downtown, on 18% of the
land, has **39**. Etobicoke–York did not have one warming or surge site open on
any of the 260 coldest nights in six years.

## The auditor looked at one winter. We looked at six.

The audit covers 2023/24. We went through every night of six winters of the
City's published records, 2020 through 2026, to find out whether that winter was
unusual. It was not.

**There is no room on the cold nights.** On nights at or below −5 °C, the walk-in
system was effectively full on **46.7%** of them. On milder nights, 20.2%. The
extra space the City opens for the cold is already out of beds by the time the
cold arrives.

**When the City closes a surge site, more people are left with nowhere.** We
compared each closure against other nights at the same temperature. After a
closure the queue of people with no bed rose by about **25 people**, and about
**11 fewer** people were placed. No beds opened anywhere else to take them. The
City did not move the capacity. It removed it.

**One quarter of the city has never had a warming centre.** Etobicoke–York went
without a single warming or surge site open on all 260 of the coldest nights in
six years.

None of this is one bad winter. It is how the system is built.

## They were told to fix it. Then they did it again.

In February 2025 the Auditor General made fifteen recommendations. The City
accepted every one. Council adopted them in March.

The next winter the City pulled its surge beds **nine times**, more than in any
season before. **Eight of those nine** were on nights at or below −5 °C. One was
at −15.7 °C. **323 beds** taken out of service on nights cold enough to kill
someone.

Turnaways are still not counted.

On the public record, the City has not changed the practice it agreed to change.

## They were paid to keep those beds open

The City paid operators the maximum **$12.5 million** for that winter, budgeted
on every bed being in use all season.

> "TSSS had budgeted for Warming Centres to be open and operating at full
> capacity for the entire 2023/24 season."

Operators reported $9.7 million in costs. Nearly **$2.9 million** had still not
been recovered a year later.

The money was there to keep the doors open. The doors were shut anyway.

## What has to stop

Shelter should not close because the weather changed. Capacity should not be
withdrawn on nights people are outside. And demand should not be measured in a
way that cannot see the person turned away at the door.

What is needed is a place for every person, every night, with no thermometer
involved. Not a lower trigger. No trigger.

This took six winters of the City's own records to establish. Those records are
public, every figure on this page can be checked against them, and the City could
have checked them at any point in the last six years.

*Sources: Auditor General of Toronto, "Audit of Toronto Shelter and Support
Services – Warming Centres and Winter Respite Sites," February 2025, pages 2–4
and Table 1. City of Toronto 2023/24 and 2024/25 Winter Services Plans. 2024
Street Needs Assessment, Appendix A. Daily Shelter and Overnight Service
